clinicalPearls: A diffuse thickening of the ventricular endocardium by collagen and elastic fibres, most often affecting the left ventricle of infants and young children.
Presents with heart failure in infancy: breathlessness, poor feeding, failure to thrive, sweating, tachypnoea and recurrent chest infections.
Two classic forms are described, a dilated type with a large poorly contracting left ventricle and a rarer contracted (restrictive) type with a small cavity.
The primary form arises without another structural lesion, whereas the secondary form accompanies congenital defects such as hypoplastic left heart, aortic stenosis or coarctation.
Echocardiography shows a brightly echogenic, thickened endocardium with a dilated hypocontractile ventricle, mitral regurgitation and impaired systolic function.
It is a recognised outcome of intrauterine insults, notably maternal anti-Ro/anti-La antibodies and viral myocarditis, and rare inherited metabolic disorders.
Endocardial thickening restricts diastolic filling and impairs contraction, driving progressive congestive cardiac failure and mural thrombus formation.
Management centres on heart failure therapy and treating any underlying cause; refractory disease may require transplantation.
reference.pathophysiology: Endocardial fibroelastosis is characterised by a diffuse, glistening, pearly-white thickening of the mural endocardium produced by a dense proliferation of collagen and elastic fibres, predominantly involving the left ventricle and often extending onto the mitral and aortic valve apparatus. The fibroelastic layer encases the ventricular wall, impairing both diastolic relaxation and systolic contraction and thereby generating heart failure. Rather than a single disease, it represents a final common endocardial response to a range of intrauterine and early-life myocardial insults. Proposed and established mechanisms include haemodynamic stress and subendocardial ischaemia in the setting of obstructive congenital lesions (the secondary form seen with hypoplastic left heart, critical aortic stenosis and coarctation), intrauterine viral myocarditis, and immune-mediated injury from transplacental passage of maternal anti-Ro and anti-La antibodies, the same antibodies implicated in congenital heart block. Lymphatic obstruction, endocardial hypoxia and abnormal wall stress have all been invoked to explain the reactive fibroelastic transformation. Certain inherited metabolic and mitochondrial disorders, as well as genetic mutations affecting the tafazzin gene and carnitine metabolism, can produce a similar phenotype. The thickened, poorly compliant endocardium promotes chamber dilatation or restriction depending on the subtype, predisposes to mural thrombus and systemic embolism, and, when the underlying process is progressive, culminates in intractable congestive failure.
additionalDifferentials: Anomalous origin of the left coronary artery from the pulmonary artery
Glycogen storage and other metabolic cardiomyopathies (including Pompe disease)
Congenital obstructive left heart lesions with secondary changes
Restrictive cardiomyopathy and cardiac involvement in mucopolysaccharidoses
additionalInvestigations: Transthoracic echocardiography assessing endocardial echogenicity, chamber size and systolic function
Electrocardiography looking for left ventricular hypertrophy, strain and repolarisation change
Maternal and infant anti-Ro and anti-La antibody testing
Cardiac MRI for tissue characterisation and quantification of fibrosis
Metabolic and genetic screening including carnitine, organic acids and targeted gene panels
Viral studies and, where indicated, endomyocardial biopsy
Coronary imaging to exclude anomalous left coronary artery
redFlags: Rapidly progressive heart failure with cardiogenic shock in an infant
Malignant arrhythmia or complete heart block
Failure to thrive with recurrent respiratory decompensation
Signs of an untreated obstructive congenital lesion driving the process
reference.prognosis: Outcome varies with subtype and cause; some children stabilise and improve with sustained heart failure therapy, while the contracted form and progressive cases carry a poor prognosis and may require transplantation. Early treatment of a reversible underlying cause improves survival.
pitfalls: Labelling the condition primary without excluding obstructive congenital lesions or anomalous coronary anatomy
Overlooking maternal autoantibodies as a treatable and preventable cause
Missing an underlying metabolic or mitochondrial disorder amenable to specific therapy
Underestimating thromboembolic risk from the abnormal endocardium
Attributing all infantile heart failure to viral illness and delaying echocardiography
references: Moss and Adams' Heart Disease in Infants, Children and Adolescents (standard reference)
management: Treat the resulting heart failure with diuretics, afterload reduction using ACE inhibitors and other guideline-directed anti-failure therapy, often sustained over years

Identify and treat a reversible underlying cause, including obstructive congenital lesions such as hypoplastic left heart, aortic stenosis or coarctation, and maternal anti-Ro/anti-La-associated disease
Screen for inherited metabolic disorders and provide appropriate substrate or cofactor replacement where a treatable cause such as carnitine deficiency is identified
Monitor ventricular function and mitral regurgitation with serial echocardiography and adjust therapy accordingly
Manage acute decompensation with inotropic support and intensive supportive care
Refer to paediatric cardiology and evaluate refractory or contracted-type disease for cardiac transplantation
Provide metabolic and genetic counselling where an inherited disorder is identified, and consider maternal autoantibody assessment in future pregnancies
